transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

Potentially, yes — but it is not automatically an uneconomic repair. On a Bosch dishwasher, E:09 means the machine has detected a fault in its flow-through heating circuit. Together with a genuinely stone-cold wash, the leading suspect is the heater assembly, which on many Bosch machines is incorporated into the circulation-pump unit rather than being a simple separate element. That can be a moderate-to-expensive repair because it may involve a substantial pump/heater assembly and labour. The cheaper possibilities are the temperature sensor or wiring connection; the control board is less likely and should only be considered after the heater circuit has been tested. This is not the usual rinse-aid or poor-drying issue: hot-but-wet dishes would be normal drying behaviour, but cold dishes plus E:09 points to a genuine heating fault. 1. Switch the dishwasher off and unplug it before any inspection. You can remove and rinse the bottom filter, mainly to make sure water circulation is not restricted; it will not usually cure an E:09, but it is worthwhile basic maintenance.
2. Avoid repeatedly running hot programmes to try to clear the code. If E:09 returns and the wash remains cold, an engineer should test the heater circuit, sensor and wiring with the machine isolated before any part is chosen. If the programme is also taking much longer than normal, that adds weight to a heater/temperature-sensing fault. If repair cost approaches a large fraction of replacement cost, ask for a fixed-price diagnosis and quote first, as the pump/heater assembly can make the decision less clear-cut.
[Helpful to see: image "Where the filter is" — The filter sits in the base of the dishwasher, usually under the bottom spray arm. Twist it out anticlockwise and rinse it under a tap. Typical layout — your dishwasher may differ.]

Thanks. I've done the filter and it's clean. I've got a multimeter, so I could check the heater resistance if that's safe to do. Roughly what would a repair cost, and is it worth it on a 9 year old machine?

On a nine-year-old Bosch, it is worth getting a diagnosis/quote, but it is borderline if the complete pump/heater unit is needed. Typical UK ballpark figures are:
1. 2. 3. E:09 plus a completely cold wash makes the heater circuit the leading cause, rather than the clean filter. You can check the heater resistance if you are confident accessing it, but only with the dishwasher switched off, unplugged and with the water isolated. Pull it out carefully with towels ready, and do not run it with any panel removed. 1. Remove only the necessary outer panel(s); do not disturb wiring unnecessarily. Photograph connections first.
2. Find the two heavier wires feeding the heater/heat-pump assembly. Disconnect at least one heater lead, so the meter is not reading through another circuit.
3. Set the meter to resistance and measure across the two heater terminals. A healthy heater usually shows a finite low-to-mid resistance reading, commonly in the tens of ohms. An open-circuit/OL reading strongly supports a failed heater assembly.
4. If you cannot identify the heater terminals with certainty, stop there and have an engineer test it. Do not probe or reconnect anything while powered. A finite resistance would not completely clear the heater system: it would move suspicion to the temperature sensor, wiring/connector or, last of all, the control board. An OL reading would make the heater/heat-pump assembly the likely repair.
Thanks. The cost figures in your reply came through blank, just "1. 2. 3.", so could you resend them? I'll try the heater check with the machine unplugged and the panel off.

Typical UK ballparks, including labour, are: 1. 2. 3. 4. E:09 plus a completely cold wash makes the heater circuit the leading fault. A resistance test is a useful way to separate an open heater from sensor/wiring/control issues. With it unplugged and isolated, an OL/open-circuit reading strongly supports the flow-through heater assembly being faulty. A finite, stable resistance in the tens of ohms does not clear the system, but makes the sensor, wiring/connector and then the control board more relevant. Take a photo of the connections before disconnecting anything, and only reconnect it with the machine fully reassembled and panels back on.
The cost figures are still blank, just "1. 2. 3. 4." with no numbers. Could you write them out in a sentence instead? I'll do the resistance check meanwhile.

Costs vary by area and whether the engineer charges a separate call-out. Get a fixed quote before authorising the repair. E:09 together with a stone-cold wash still puts the flow-through heater circuit first. Your resistance check is the useful separator: OL/open circuit points to the heater/pump assembly; a stable finite reading, usually in the tens of ohms, shifts suspicion towards the temperature sensor, wiring connection or—less commonly—the control board. Keep it unplugged while disconnecting or reconnecting anything, and refit all panels before restoring power.

Ok, I've done the resistance check across the heater terminals on the pump and it reads open circuit. So is the heater/pump unit the problem? Still no cost figures from you, so I'll get a fixed quote, but is it likely worth it on a 9 year old machine?

[Heading: Likely cause: heater]
Where the heater is integral to the circulation-pump assembly, the usual repair is replacement of that complete pump/heater unit, rather than a separate element. Wiring or the control board would not normally make the heater itself read open circuit. Ask for the total including diagnosis, parts, labour, VAT and any return visit before approving it. I cannot confirm an exact parts match from the supplied model number alone, so let the engineer or Bosch spares service verify it from the rating plate before ordering. The open-circuit result means a fixed quote is justified; there is little value in spending more time chasing the sensor or PCB first. This is now an internal pump/heater replacement rather than a basic owner repair, so keep it isolated and have an engineer carry out the replacement.
